Distribution of named [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") in the [Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_System "Solar System") as of 2017.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

This is a list of [craters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impact_crater "Impact crater") on [Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venus "Venus"), [named](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetary_nomenclature "Planetary nomenclature") by the [International Astronomical Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Astronomical_Union "International Astronomical Union")'s (IAU) [Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_Group_for_Planetary_System_Nomenclature "Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature"). All craters on Venus are named after famous women or female first names.[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1)[[5]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Categories-6) *(For features on Venus other than craters see, [list of montes on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_montes_on_Venus "List of montes on Venus") and [List of coronae on Venus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_coronae_on_Venus "List of coronae on Venus").[[6]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Target-Venus-7))*

As of 2017, there are 900 named craters on Venus,[[1]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Venus-Craterlist-1) fewer than the [lunar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_the_Moon "List of craters on the Moon") and [Martian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mars "List of craters on Mars") craters but more than [on Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Mercury "List of craters on Mercury").[[2]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mercury-Craterlist-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Moon-Craterlist-3)[[4]](#cite_note-Gazetteer-Mars-Craterlist-4)[[a]](#cite_note-WGPSN-Dropped-5)

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include [Callisto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callisto_(moon) "Callisto (moon)") ([141](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Callisto "List of craters on Callisto")), [Ganymede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ganymede_(moon) "Ganymede (moon)") ([131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Ganymede "List of craters on Ganymede")), [Rhea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhea_(moon) "Rhea (moon)") (128), [Vesta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_Vesta "4 Vesta") (90), [Ceres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceres_(dwarf_planet) "Ceres (dwarf planet)") (90), [Dione](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dione_(moon) "Dione (moon)") (73), [Iapetus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iapetus_(moon) "Iapetus (moon)") (58), [Enceladus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enceladus_(moon) "Enceladus (moon)") (53), [Tethys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tethys_(moon) "Tethys (moon)") (50) and [Europa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europa_(moon) "Europa (moon)") ([41](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_on_Europa "List of craters on Europa")). For a full list, *see [List of craters in the Solar System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_craters_in_the_Solar_System "List of craters in the Solar System")*.

[![Photograph of Pierre de Coubertin](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ef/Baron_Pierre_de_Coubertin.jpg/250px-Baron_Pierre_de_Coubertin.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Baron_Pierre_de_Coubertin.jpg)

Under the pseudonyms Georges Hohrod and Martin Eschbach, [IOC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") founder [Pierre de Coubertin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_de_Coubertin "Pierre de Coubertin") won a gold medal in the literature category at the [1912 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_1912_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the 1912 Summer Olympics").

There were 146 medalists in [the art competitions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_competitions_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Art competitions at the Summer Olympics") that were part of the [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") from [1912](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1912_Summer_Olympics "1912 Summer Olympics") until [1948](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1948_Summer_Olympics "1948 Summer Olympics"). These art competitions were considered an integral part of the movement by [International Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") (IOC) founder [Pierre de Coubertin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_de_Coubertin "Pierre de Coubertin") and necessary to recapture the complete essence of the [Ancient Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Olympic_Games "Ancient Olympic Games"). Their absence before the [1912 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1912_Summer_Olympics "1912 Summer Olympics"), according to journalism professor Richard Stanton, stems from Coubertin "not wanting to fragment the focus of his new and fragile movement".[[1]](#cite_note-Stanton3-1) Art competitions were originally planned for inclusion in the [1908 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_Summer_Olympics "1908 Summer Olympics") but were delayed after that edition's change in venue from Rome to London following the 1906 eruption of [Mount Vesuvius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Vesuvius "Mount Vesuvius").[[2]](#cite_note-Stanton18-2) By the [1924 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1924_Summer_Olympics "1924 Summer Olympics") they had grown to be considered internationally relevant and potentially "a milestone in advancing public awareness of art as a whole".[[3]](#cite_note-Stanton69-3)

During their first three appearances, the art competitions were grouped into five broad categories: architecture, literature, music, painting, and sculpture. The Dutch Organizing Committee for the [1928 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1928_Summer_Olympics "1928 Summer Olympics") split these into subcategories in the hopes of increasing participation.[[4]](#cite_note-Stanton95-4) Although it was a successful strategy, the [1932 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1932_Summer_Olympics "1932 Summer Olympics") eliminated several of these subcategories, which led to fewer entries in the broader categories.[[5]](#cite_note-Stanton146-5) For the [1936 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1936_Summer_Olympics "1936 Summer Olympics"), the German government proposed the addition of a film contest to the program, which was rejected.[[6]](#cite_note-Stanton158-6)

Following a final appearance at the [1948 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1948_Summer_Olympics "1948 Summer Olympics"), art competitions were removed from the Olympic program. Planners of the [1952 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1952_Summer_Olympics "1952 Summer Olympics") opposed their inclusion on logistical grounds, claiming that the lack of an international association for the event meant that the entire onus of facilitation was placed on the local organizing committee.[[7]](#cite_note-Stanton210-7) Concerns were also raised about the professionalism of the event, since only amateurs were allowed to participate in the sporting tournaments,[[8]](#cite_note-Stanton211-8) and the growing commercialization of the competitions, as artists had been permitted to sell their submissions during the course of the Games since 1928. In 1952 an art festival and exhibition was held concurrent with the Games, a tradition that has been maintained in all subsequent Summer [Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games").[[9]](#cite_note-Stanton213-9)

In 1952, art competition medals were removed from the official national medal counts.[[10]](#cite_note-e048-10) The IOC does not track medalists in Olympic art competitions in its database and thus the prize winners are only officially recorded in the original Olympic reports. Judges were not required to distribute first, second, and third place awards for every category, and thus certain events lack medalists in these placements. Since participants were allowed multiple submissions, it was also possible for artists to win more than one in a single event, as [Alex Diggelmann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Diggelmann "Alex Diggelmann") of Switzerland did in the graphic arts category of the 1948 edition.[[11]](#cite_note-1948_Report-11) Diggelmann is tied with Denmark's [Josef Petersen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josef_Petersen "Josef Petersen"), who won second prize three times in literature, for the number of medals captured in the art competitions. Luxembourg's [Jean Jacoby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Jacoby "Jean Jacoby") is the only individual to win two gold medals, doing so in painting in 1924 and 1928. Of the 146 medalists, 11 were women and only Finnish author [Aale Tynni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aale_Tynni "Aale Tynni") was awarded gold. Germany was the most successful nation, with eight gold, seven silver, and nine bronze medals,[[12]](#cite_note-SRArt-12) although one was won by Coubertin himself, a Frenchman. He submitted his poem *Ode to Sport* under the pseudonyms Georges Hohrod and Martin Eschbach, as if it were a joint-entry, and won first prize in the 1912 literature category. The original report credits this medal to Germany.[[13]](#cite_note-Coubertin-13) Two individuals, [Walter W. Winans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_W._Winans "Walter W. Winans")[[14]](#cite_note-Winans-14) and [Alfréd Hajós](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfréd_Hajós "Alfréd Hajós"), won medals in both athletic and art competitions.[[15]](#cite_note-Hajos-15)

Art competitions formed part of the modern [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") during its early years, from 1912 to 1948. The competitions were part of the original intention of the Olympic Movement's founder, [Pierre de Frédy, Baron de Coubertin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_de_Coubertin "Pierre de Coubertin"). Medals were awarded for works of art inspired by [sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport "Sport"), divided into five categories: [architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture "Architecture"), [literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literature "Literature"), [music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music "Music"), [painting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Painting "Painting"), and [sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sculpture "Sculpture"),[[1]](#cite_note-:0-1) which led to the events' initial moniker of "Pentathlon of the Muses".[[2]](#cite_note-smithsonianmag.com-2)

The [juried](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juried_(competition) "Juried (competition)") art competitions halted after a 1949 decision by the [IOC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") that since the majority of art contestants worked as professional artists, the competitions contradicted the Olympic spirit of amateur competition, which was more strictly enforced for athletes. Art exhibitions replaced the competitions in the following years, and since 1956, host nations have organized [Cultural Olympiads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Olympiad "Cultural Olympiad") at their own discretion.[[3]](#cite_note-:1-3)

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Art_competitions_at_the_Summer_Olympics&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

With the founding of the [International Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") (IOC) in 1894, and the celebration of the [first modern Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1896_Summer_Olympics "1896 Summer Olympics"), French Baron Pierre de Coubertin saw the fulfillment of his ideals—men being educated in both mind and body, and competing in sport rather than war. One of his other desires was to combine both art and sport, and he thus considered including artistic competition in the Olympic Games.

De Coubertin became the driving force for promoting the arts through the Olympics, and in 1904, he wrote the following in the French newspaper *[Le Figaro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Figaro "Le Figaro")*: "The time has come to take the next step, and to restore the Olympiad to its original beauty. In the high times of Olympia, the fine arts were combined harmoniously with the Olympic Games to create their glory. This is to become reality once again."[[3]](#cite_note-:1-3)

Support for the art competitions grew, and in May 1906, Baron de Coubertin organised a meeting in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") for both IOC members and representatives of artists' organisations. The meeting ended with a proposal to the IOC to organise artistic competitions at the Olympic Games in five areas (architecture, literature, music, painting, and sculpture). The works of art entered had to be inspired by sports.

Preparations were underway to hold such competitions at the [1908 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1908_Summer_Olympics "1908 Summer Olympics"), which were scheduled for [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome"), [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"). But the Italian organisers faced severe difficulties due to the [Vesuvius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Vesuvius "Mount Vesuvius") volcano eruption of 1906, which forced them to halt preparations, and the IOC awarded the organisation to [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London") in 1907. The British organisers planned to hold the art competitions, but because of the short preparation time, they were cancelled. The organisers felt that artists would not have enough time to send in their works.[[2]](#cite_note-smithsonianmag.com-2)

Pierre de Coubertin was not discouraged, and sought to include the artistic events in the programme of the [1912 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1912_Summer_Olympics "1912 Summer Olympics"), to be held in [Stockholm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm "Stockholm"), [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden "Sweden"). Although the Swedes initially objected, opposing the idea of art combined with competition, they eventually gave in. The number of entrants was rather disappointing: only 35 artists are known to have sent works of art to Sweden, but gold medals were awarded in all five categories.

The [1916 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1916_Summer_Olympics "1916 Summer Olympics") were planned in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin"), but [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") caused the events to be cancelled. Coubertin lobbied hard to host the games despite the war, trying to invoke the ancient Greek concept of "[Ekeheiria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ekecheiria "Ekecheiria")" (laying down of arms). During the ancient Greek games, this sacred truce allowed for free travel and participation in the Games regardless of conflicts. Coubertin believed that continuing with the Games as planned in Berlin would possibly contribute to a halt in the war. However, opposition to Germany as the host proved too strong, and governments were not willing to pause the conflict. Thus, the 1916 Games were cancelled.[[4]](#cite_note-4)

When the first [post-war Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1920_Summer_Olympics "1920 Summer Olympics") were held in war-ravaged [Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium"), art contests were again on the programme, though it wasn't until the [1924 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1924_Summer_Olympics "1924 Summer Olympics") in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris") that the arts were featured prominently.[[5]](#cite_note-5) The contests were taken seriously for the first time, and 193 artists submitted works, which included three [Russian émigré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_émigré "White émigré") artists. The [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") officially did not take part in the Olympic Games, which they considered to be a "bourgeois" festival.

The growth continued at the [1928 Amsterdam Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1928_Summer_Olympics "1928 Summer Olympics"), where over 1,100 works of art were exhibited in the [Municipal Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stedelijk_Museum "Stedelijk Museum"), not including the submissions in literature, music and architecture. Artists were allowed to sell their works at the close of the exhibition, which was rather controversial given the IOC's amateurism policy, which required all competitors to be amateurs. In Amsterdam, the number of events was also increased, as four of the five fields of art were subdivided, creating more events.

Because of the economy and the remote location of [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), participation in the athletic events of the [1932 Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1932_Summer_Olympics "1932 Summer Olympics") was lower than that of 1928. The art competition did not suffer from this problem, and the number of art works entered remained stable. Their exhibition drew 384,000 visitors to the [Los Angeles Museum of History, Science and Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Museum_of_History,_Science_and_Art "Los Angeles Museum of History, Science and Art"). Art contests were also held in [Berlin (1936)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1936_Summer_Olympics "1936 Summer Olympics") and [London (1948)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1948_Summer_Olympics "1948 Summer Olympics"), with reasonable success, although the number of entered works had significantly dropped by 1948.

In 1949, a report was presented at the IOC meeting in Rome concluded that since practically all contestants in the art competitions were professionals, the competitions should be abolished and replaced with an exhibition without awards or medals. This sparked a heated debate within the IOC. At a 1951 meeting, the IOC decided to reinstate the competitions for the [1952 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1952_Summer_Olympics "1952 Summer Olympics") in [Helsinki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki "Helsinki"). However, the organisers claimed there was insufficient time, and an art competition was not held. An art exhibition took place in its stead.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

The issue continued to be debated within the Olympic Movement, and at the 49th IOC Session in Athens, 1954, the IOC members voted to replace the art contests with an exhibition for future Olympics. Several attempts have been made to re-include them, but without success.

Despite no longer holding art competitions, the Olympic games continue to be connected with art exhibitions. The [Olympic Charter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Charter "Olympic Charter") required organisers of the Olympic Games to include a programme of cultural events, to "serve to promote harmonious relations, mutual understanding and friendship among the participants and others attending the Olympic Games."

Many of the art winners and entries have been lost to time. Two famous works that historians have been unable to find include "A Rider’s Instructions to His Lover" by the German poet Rudolf Binding, which won the silver medal in literature at the 1928 Amsterdam Games, and "Before the Gods of Olympia" by the French rugby player Charles Gonnet. Many architectural designs have also been lost.[[7]](#cite_note-ReferenceA-7)

**Sonja Henie** (8 April 1912 – 12 October 1969) was a Norwegian [figure skater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Figure_skating "Figure skating") and film star. She was a three-time [Olympic champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_medalists_in_figure_skating "List of Olympic medalists in figure skating") ([1928](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Figure_skating_at_the_1928_Winter_Olympics "Figure skating at the 1928 Winter Olympics"), [1932](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Figure_skating_at_the_1932_Winter_Olympics "Figure skating at the 1932 Winter Olympics"), [1936](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Figure_skating_at_the_1936_Winter_Olympics "Figure skating at the 1936 Winter Olympics")) in women's [singles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single_skating "Single skating"), a ten-time [World champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Figure_Skating_Championships "World Figure Skating Championships") (1927–1936) and a six-time [European champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Figure_Skating_Championships "European Figure Skating Championships") (1931–1936). Henie won more Olympic and World titles than any other ladies' figure skater. She is one of only two skaters to successfully defend a ladies' singles Olympic title, the other being [Katarina Witt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katarina_Witt "Katarina Witt"), and her six consecutive European titles have only been matched by Witt.

At the height of Henie's American acting career, she was one of the highest-paid stars in [Hollywood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinema_in_the_United_States "Cinema in the United States") and starred in a series of box-office hits, including *[Thin Ice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thin_Ice_(1937_film) "Thin Ice (1937 film)")* (1937), *[Happy Landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Happy_Landing_(1938_film) "Happy Landing (1938 film)")* (1938), *[My Lucky Star](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Lucky_Star_(1938_film) "My Lucky Star (1938 film)")* (1938), *[Second Fiddle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Fiddle_(1939_film) "Second Fiddle (1939 film)")* (1939), and *[Sun Valley Serenade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sun_Valley_Serenade "Sun Valley Serenade")* (1941).[[1]](#cite_note-snlno-1)

## Biography

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Sonja_Henie&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

### Early life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Sonja_Henie&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Early life")]

Henie was born on 8 April 1912 in Kristiania (now [Oslo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oslo "Oslo")), Norway; she was the only daughter of [Wilhelm Henie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_Henie "Wilhelm Henie") (1872–1937), a prosperous Norwegian [furrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fur_clothing "Fur clothing"), and his wife, Selma Lochmann-Nielsen (1888–1961). In addition to the income from the fur business, both of Henie's parents had inherited wealth. Wilhelm Henie had been a one-time [World Cycling Champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCI_Track_Cycling_World_Championships "UCI Track Cycling World Championships") and the Henie children were encouraged to take up a variety of sports at a young age. Henie initially showed talent at [skiing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skiing "Skiing"), then followed her older brother, Leif, to take up [figure skating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Figure_skating "Figure skating"). As a girl Henie also was a nationally ranked [tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis "Tennis") player, and a skilled [swimmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_(sport) "Swimming (sport)") and [equestrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equestrianism "Equestrianism"). Once Henie began serious training as a figure skater, her formal schooling ended. She was educated by tutors, and her father hired the best experts in the world, including the famous Russian ballerina, [Tamara Karsavina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamara_Karsavina "Tamara Karsavina"), to transform his daughter into a sporting celebrity.[[1]](#cite_note-snlno-1)

Henie began skating at the age of 5. She enjoyed music and dance from an early age, studying [ballet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballet "Ballet") and after starting her competitive skating career, admired the Russian ballet dancer [Anna Pavlova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Pavlova "Anna Pavlova") after seeing her perform in London.[[2]](#cite_note-kestnbaum-106-2)

### Competitive career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Sonja_Henie&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Competitive career")]

Henie skating with [Arne Lie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne_Lie_(figure_skater)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Arne Lie (figure skater) (page does not exist)") [[no](https://no.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arne%20Lie%20(kunstløper) "no:Arne Lie (kunstløper)")] in 1925

Henie with British skater [Cecilia Colledge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cecilia_Colledge "Cecilia Colledge") during the medals ceremony at the 1936 Olympics in Garmisch-Partenkirchen.

Henie placed eighth in a field of eight at the [1924 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1924_Winter_Olympics "1924 Winter Olympics"), at the age of eleven.[[3]](#cite_note-sr-3) Henie won the first of an unprecedented ten consecutive World Figure Skating Championships in 1927 at the age of fourteen.[[4]](#cite_note-hines-xxiii-4) The results of 1927 World Championships, where Henie won in 3–2 decision (or 7 vs. 8 ordinal points) over the defending Olympic and World Champion [Herma Szabo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herma_Szabo "Herma Szabo") of [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria"), was "controversial",[[4]](#cite_note-hines-xxiii-4) as three of the five judges that gave Henie first-place ordinals were Norwegian (1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 7 points) while Szabo received first-place ordinals from an Austrian and a German judge (1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8 points). Henie went on to win the first of her three [Olympic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") gold medals the following year, becoming one of the youngest figure skating Olympic champions. She defended her Olympic titles in 1932 and in 1936, and her world titles annually until 1936. Henie and [Gillis Grafström](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gillis_Grafström "Gillis Grafström") from Sweden are the only skaters to win three Olympic gold medals in single skating.[[3]](#cite_note-sr-3)[[4]](#cite_note-hines-xxiii-4) She also won six consecutive European championships from 1931 to 1936.

**Francina Elsje** "**Fanny**" **Blankers-Koen** (pronounced [[frɑnˈsinaː ˈʔɛlɕə ˈfɑni ˈblɑŋkərs ˈkun]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Dutch "Help:IPA/Dutch") [ⓘ](/wiki/File:Fanny-blankers-koen-by-anne-roos-lieven-2024-02.oga "File:Fanny-blankers-koen-by-anne-roos-lieven-2024-02.oga"); née **Koen**, 26 April 1918 – 25 January 2004) was a Dutch [track and field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_and_field "Track and field") athlete, best known for winning four gold medals at the [1948 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1948_Summer_Olympics "1948 Summer Olympics") in London. She competed there as a 30-year-old mother of two, earning her the nickname "**the Flying Housewife**", and was the most successful athlete at the event.[[1]](#cite_note-guardianolysrs-1)

Having started competing in athletics in 1935, she took part in the [1936 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1936_Summer_Olympics "1936 Summer Olympics") a year later. Although international competition was stopped by World War II, Blankers-Koen set several world records during that period, in events as diverse as the [long jump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_jump "Long jump"), the [high jump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_jump "High jump"), and [sprint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprint_(running) "Sprint (running)") and [hurdling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurdling "Hurdling") events.

Apart from her four Olympic titles, she won five [European titles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Athletics_Championships "European Athletics Championships") and 58 Dutch championships, and set or tied 12 world records – the last, in the [pentathlon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentathlon "Pentathlon"), in 1951 aged 33. She retired from athletics in 1955, after which she became captain of the Dutch female track and field team. In 1999, she was voted "Female Athlete of the Century" by the [International Association of Athletics Federations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Association_of_Athletics_Federations "International Association of Athletics Federations") (IAAF). Her Olympic victories are credited with helping to eliminate the belief that age and motherhood were barriers to success in women's sport.[[1]](#cite_note-guardianolysrs-1)

## Early life

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Fanny_Blankers-Koen&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Fanny Koen was born on 26 April 1918 in [Lage Vuursche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lage_Vuursche "Lage Vuursche") (near [Baarn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baarn "Baarn")) to Arnoldus and Helena Koen. Her father was a government official who competed in the [shot put](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shot_put "Shot put") and [discus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discus "Discus").[[2]](#cite_note-indyobit-2) She had five brothers.[[2]](#cite_note-indyobit-2) As a teenager, she enjoyed [tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis "Tennis"), swimming, [gymnastics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gymnastics "Gymnastics"), [ice skating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ice_skating "Ice skating"), [fencing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fencing "Fencing") and [running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Running "Running"). Standing 1.75 m (5 ft 9 in), she was a natural athlete. It soon became clear she had a talent for sports, but she could not decide which sport to pick. A swimming coach advised her to concentrate on running because there were already several top swimmers in the Netherlands at that time (such as [Rie Mastenbroek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rie_Mastenbroek "Rie Mastenbroek")), and she would have a better chance to qualify for the Olympics in a track event.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

Her first appearance in the sport was in 1935, aged 17.[[3]](#cite_note-bbcprofile-3) Her first competition was a disappointment, but in her third race, she set a national record in the 800 m. Fanny Koen soon made the Dutch team, although as a sprinter, not a middle-distance runner. At that time, 800 m was generally considered too physically demanding for female contestants and had been removed from the Olympic programme after 1928.[[1]](#cite_note-guardianolysrs-1)[[2]](#cite_note-indyobit-2) The following year, her coach and future husband, [Jan Blankers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Blankers "Jan Blankers"), a former Olympic [triple-jumper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple-jump "Triple-jump") who had participated in the [1928 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1928_Summer_Olympics "1928 Summer Olympics"), encouraged her to enter the trials for the [1936 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1936_Summer_Olympics "1936 Summer Olympics") in Berlin.[[3]](#cite_note-bbcprofile-3) At eighteen years old, she was selected to compete in the [high jump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_jump "High jump") and the 4 × 100 m [relay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Relay_race "Relay race").[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

At the Berlin Olympics, the high jump and the 4 × 100 m relay competitions were held on the same day. In the high jump, she took fifth place (shared with two other jumpers), while the Dutch relay team came in fifth in the final (the sixth team in the final, Germany, was disqualified).[[4]](#cite_note-iaaf-4) She also obtained the [autograph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autograph "Autograph") of American athlete [Jesse Owens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Owens "Jesse Owens"); it became her most treasured possession.[[2]](#cite_note-indyobit-2)[[5]](#cite_note-observer-5)

Slowly, Koen rose to the top. In 1938, she ran her first world record (11.0 seconds in the 100 yards), and she also won her first international medals. At the European Championships in Vienna, she won the bronze in both the 100 and 200 m,[[6]](#cite_note-r1-6) which were both won by [Stanisława Walasiewicz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanisława_Walasiewicz "Stanisława Walasiewicz"). Many observers, and Koen herself, expected her to do well at the upcoming [Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1940_Summer_Olympics "1940 Summer Olympics"), which were due to be held in Helsinki in July 1940.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

However, the outbreak of World War II put a stop to the preparations. The Olympics were formally cancelled on 2 May 1940, a week before [the Netherlands was invaded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Netherlands "Battle of the Netherlands").[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

**Mildred Ella** "**Babe**" **Didrikson Zaharias** ([/zəˈhæriəs/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); [née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name") **Didrikson**; June 26, 1911 – September 27, 1956) was an American athlete who excelled in [golf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golf "Golf"), [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball"), [baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball "Baseball"), and [track and field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_and_field "Track and field"). She won two gold medals and a silver in track and field at the [1932 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1932_Summer_Olympics "1932 Summer Olympics") before turning to professional golf and winning 10 [LPGA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LPGA "LPGA") major championships.

## Biography

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Babe_Didrikson_Zaharias&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Biography")]

Mildred Ella Didrikson was born on June 26, 1911,[[3]](#cite_note-Gianoulis-3) the sixth of seven children, in the coastal [city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City "City") of [Port Arthur, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Arthur,_Texas "Port Arthur, Texas"). Her mother Hannah and her father Ole Didriksen were immigrants from [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway "Norway"). Although her three eldest siblings were born in Norway, Babe and her three other siblings were born in Port Arthur. She later changed the spelling of her surname from Didriksen to Didrikson.[[4]](#cite_note-ESPN-4) She moved with her family to 850 Doucette in [Beaumont, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaumont,_Texas "Beaumont, Texas"), at age 4. She claimed to have acquired the nickname "Babe" (after [Babe Ruth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babe_Ruth "Babe Ruth")) upon hitting five [home runs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_run "Home run") in a childhood [baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baseball "Baseball") game, but her Norwegian mother had called her "Bebe" from the time she was a toddler.[[5]](#cite_note-wondergirl-5)

Although best known for her athletic gifts, Didrikson had many talents. She also competed in sewing. An excellent [seamstress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seamstress "Seamstress"), she made many of her clothes, including her golfing outfits. She claimed to have won the sewing championship at the 1931 [State Fair of Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Fair_of_Texas "State Fair of Texas") in [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas"); she did win the [South Texas State Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Texas_State_Fair "South Texas State Fair") in Beaumont, embellishing the story many years later in 1953. She attended Beaumont High School. Never a strong student, she was forced to repeat the eighth grade and was a year older than her classmates. She eventually dropped out without graduating after she moved to Dallas to play basketball.[[5]](#cite_note-wondergirl-5) She was a singer and a [harmonica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonica "Harmonica") player and recorded several songs on the [Mercury Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mercury_Records "Mercury Records") label. Her biggest seller was "I Felt a Little Teardrop" with "Detour" on the flip side.[[6]](#cite_note-teardrop-6)

Already famous as Babe Didrikson, she married [George Zaharias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Zaharias "George Zaharias") (1908–1984), a professional [wrestler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wrestler "Wrestler"), in [St. Louis, Missouri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Louis,_Missouri "St. Louis, Missouri"), on December 23, 1938. Thereafter, she was largely known as **Babe Didrikson Zaharias** or **Babe Zaharias**.[[7]](#cite_note-7)

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Babe_Zaharias_Park_IMG_1064.JPG/250px-Babe_Zaharias_Park_IMG_1064.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Babe_Zaharias_Park_IMG_1064.JPG)

Babe Zaharias Park is located in [Beaumont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beaumont,_Texas "Beaumont, Texas") adjacent to her [museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Babe_Didrikson_Zaharias_Museum_&_Visitor_Center "Babe Didrikson Zaharias Museum & Visitor Center").

### Athletic achievements

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Babe_Didrikson_Zaharias&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Athletic achievements")]

Didrikson gained world fame in [track and field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_and_field "Track and field") and was a three-time [AAU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_Athletic_Union "Amateur Athletic Union") [All-American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-America "All-America") in basketball from 1930–1932.[[4]](#cite_note-ESPN-4) She played organized baseball and softball and was an expert diver, roller-skater, and bowler.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

#### AAU champion

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Babe_Didrikson_Zaharias&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: AAU champion")]

Didrikson's first job after high school was as a secretary for the Employers' Casualty Insurance Company of Dallas, though she was employed only in order to play [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") as an amateur on the company's "industrial team", the [Golden Cyclones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Cyclones "Golden Cyclones").[[9]](#cite_note-NPRBooks-9) As a side note, the competition was then governed by the [Amateur Athletic Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amateur_Athletic_Union "Amateur Athletic Union") (AAU). Despite leading the team to an AAU Basketball Championship in 1931,[[10]](#cite_note-Ikard33-10) Didrikson had first achieved wider attention as a track and field athlete.

**Gertrude Caroline Ederle** ([/ˈɛdərli/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); October 23, 1905 – November 30, 2003) was an American competition [swimmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_(sport) "Swimming (sport)"), Olympic champion, and world record-holder in five events. On August 6, 1926, she became the first woman to [swim across the English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swim_across_the_English_Channel "Swim across the English Channel") with her finish time of 14 hours and 45 minutes, beating the record set by [Enrique Tirabocchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrique_Tirabocchi "Enrique Tirabocchi") in 1923 by one hour, 48 minutes. Among other nicknames, the press called her "Queen of the Waves".

## Amateur career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Gertrude_Ederle&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Amateur career")]

Ederle grew up in [Manhattan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manhattan "Manhattan"), where her father ran a butcher shop on [Amsterdam Avenue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tenth_Avenue_(Manhattan) "Tenth Avenue (Manhattan)"), and learned to swim in [Highlands, New Jersey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highlands,_New_Jersey "Highlands, New Jersey").[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5): 21–22, 67, 127 She later trained at the Women's Swimming Association (WSA), founded by [Charlotte Epstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Epstein "Charlotte Epstein"). The WSA was a historic organization whose leadership and members campaigned for Women's suffrage, worked to create more swimming events open to women, and sought to increase women's participation in the Olympics. Ederle joined the club when she was only twelve and immediately took to learning the [American crawl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_crawl "American crawl"), developed at the WSA by Head Coach [Louis Handley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_Handley "Louis Handley"). The same year, she set her first world record in the 880-yard freestyle, becoming the youngest world record holder in swimming. She set eight more world records after that, seven of them in 1922 at [Brighton Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brighton_Beach "Brighton Beach").[[6]](#cite_note-sroprofile-6) In total, Ederle held 29 US national and world records from 1921 until 1925.[[7]](#cite_note-ishofprofile-7)

### 1924 Paris Olympic medalist

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Gertrude_Ederle&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: 1924 Paris Olympic medalist")]

At the [1924 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1924_Summer_Olympics "1924 Summer Olympics") in Paris, Ederle won a gold medal as a member of the U.S. team in the [4×100 meter freestyle relay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1924_Summer_Olympics_–_Women's_4_×_100_metre_freestyle_relay "Swimming at the 1924 Summer Olympics – Women's 4 × 100 metre freestyle relay"). She and teammates [Euphrasia Donnelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euphrasia_Donnelly "Euphrasia Donnelly"), [Ethel Lackie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethel_Lackie "Ethel Lackie"), and [Mariechen Wehselau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariechen_Wehselau "Mariechen Wehselau") set a world record of 4:58.8 in the event final. Individually, she received bronze medals in the [women's 100-meter freestyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1924_Summer_Olympics_–_Women's_100_metre_freestyle "Swimming at the 1924 Summer Olympics – Women's 100 metre freestyle") and [women's 400-meter freestyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1924_Summer_Olympics_–_Women's_400_metre_freestyle "Swimming at the 1924 Summer Olympics – Women's 400 metre freestyle") races.[[6]](#cite_note-sroprofile-6) The U.S. Olympic team was given a [ticker-tape parade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ticker-tape_parade "Ticker-tape parade") in 1924.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

## Professional career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Gertrude_Ederle&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Professional career")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4b/Bundesarchiv_Bild_102-10212%2C_Gertrud_Ederle.jpg/250px-Bundesarchiv_Bild_102-10212%2C_Gertrud_Ederle.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bundesarchiv_Bild_102-10212,_Gertrud_Ederle.jpg)

Gertrude Ederle: "People said women couldn't swim the Channel, but I proved they could."

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Gertrude_Ederle_parade_NYWTS.jpg/250px-Gertrude_Ederle_parade_NYWTS.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Gertrude_Ederle_parade_NYWTS.jpg)

Parade for Ederle along the [Canyon of Heroes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canyon_of_Heroes "Canyon of Heroes"), 1926

In 1925, Ederle turned professional, swimming the 22 miles (35 km) from [Battery Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battery_Park "Battery Park") to [Sandy Hook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandy_Hook,_New_Jersey "Sandy Hook, New Jersey") in 7 hours and 11 minutes, a record that stood for 81 years before being broken by Australian swimmer [Tammy van Wisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tammy_van_Wisse "Tammy van Wisse").[[9]](#cite_note-trtnj1-9) Ederle's nephew Bob later described his aunt's swim as a "midnight frolic" and a "warm-up" for her later [swim across the English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swim_across_the_English_Channel "Swim across the English Channel").[[9]](#cite_note-trtnj1-9)[[10]](#cite_note-:0-10)

### English Channel crossing

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Gertrude_Ederle&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: English Channel crossing")]

In 1925, the Women's Swimming Association sponsored [Helen Wainwright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Wainwright "Helen Wainwright") and Ederle in an attempt at swimming across the English Channel. Helen Wainwright cancelled due to an injury, but Ederle decided to try the crossing on her own. She trained with [Jabez Wolffe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jabez_Wolffe "Jabez Wolffe"), who had attempted 22 times to swim the Channel.[[11]](#cite_note-11) On August 18, 1925, Ederle made her first attempt, but she was disqualified when Wolffe ordered another swimmer, Ishak Helmy, to recover her from the water. She bitterly disagreed with Wolffe's decision, and it was speculated that he did not want Ederle to succeed.[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5): 82

She returned to New York and began training with coach [Bill Burgess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Burgess "Bill Burgess"), who had successfully swum the Channel in 1911. Ederle also received a contract from both the [New York *Daily News*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Daily_News "New York Daily News") and *[Chicago Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Tribune "Chicago Tribune")* that paid her expenses and provided her with a modest salary. Approximately one year after her first attempt, she was successful.[[12]](#cite_note-12) She started at [Cap Gris-Nez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cap_Gris-Nez "Cap Gris-Nez") in France at 07:08 am on August 6, 1926, and came ashore at [Kingsdown, Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingsdown,_Dover "Kingsdown, Dover"), 14 hours and 34 minutes later, having swum the equivalent of 35 miles due to stormy conditions taking her past her anticipated end point.[[13]](#cite_note-:2-13) The first person to greet her was a British immigration officer who requested a passport from "the bleary-eyed, waterlogged teenager".[[14]](#cite_note-14) Her record stood until [Florence Chadwick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Chadwick "Florence Chadwick") swam the Channel in 1950 in 13 hours and 23 minutes.[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5): 247

Prior to Ederle, only five men had completed the swim across the English Channel, with the best time of 16 hours, 33 minutes by [Enrique Tirabocchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrique_Tirabocchi "Enrique Tirabocchi").[[15]](#cite_note-15)

When Ederle returned home, she was greeted with a [ticker-tape parade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ticker-tape_parade "Ticker-tape parade") in Manhattan, with more than two million people along the parade route.[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5): iv, 247

### Later career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Gertrude_Ederle&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Later career")]

She made an arrangement with [Edward L. Hyman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_L._Hyman "Edward L. Hyman") to appear at the [Brooklyn Mark Strand Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strand_Theatre_(Brooklyn) "Strand Theatre (Brooklyn)"), who paid her significantly more than any prior individual performer.[[16]](#cite_note-16) Subsequently, she went on to play herself in a movie (*[Swim Girl, Swim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swim_Girl,_Swim "Swim Girl, Swim")* starring [Bebe Daniels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bebe_Daniels "Bebe Daniels")) and tour the [vaudeville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaudeville "Vaudeville") circuit, including later [Billy Rose's Aquacade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Rose's_Aquacade "Billy Rose's Aquacade"). She met [President Coolidge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_Coolidge "Calvin Coolidge") and had a song and a dance step named for her. Her manager, [Dudley Field Malone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dudley_Field_Malone "Dudley Field Malone"), was not able to capitalize on her fame and popularity, diminishing the financial potential of her vaudeville career. The [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression") also affected the success of her career. A fall down the steps of her apartment building in 1933 twisted her spine and left her bedridden for several years, but she recovered sufficiently to appear at the [1939 New York World's Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1939_New_York_World's_Fair "1939 New York World's Fair").[[5]](#cite_note-:1-5): 238–40

**Charlotte "Chattie" Reinagle Cooper Sterry** (née **Cooper**; 22 September 1870 – 10 October 1966) was an English female [tennis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis "Tennis") player who won five singles titles at the [Wimbledon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wimbledon_Championships "Wimbledon Championships") and in 1900 became Olympic champion. In winning in Paris on 11 July 1900, she became the first female Olympic tennis champion as well as the first individual female Olympic champion.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

## Early life and career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Charlotte_Cooper_(tennis)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and career")]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c4/Hillyard_vs_sterry_at_eastbourne.jpg/330px-Hillyard_vs_sterry_at_eastbourne.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hillyard_vs_sterry_at_eastbourne.jpg)

Charlotte Cooper Sterry vs Blanche Bingley Hillyard at Eastbourne

Charlotte Cooper was born on 22 September 1870 at Waldham Lodge, [Ealing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ealing "Ealing"), [Middlesex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middlesex "Middlesex"), England, the youngest daughter of Henry Cooper, a miller, and his wife Teresa Georgiana Miller.[[2]](#cite_note-odnb-2) She learned to play tennis at the Ealing Lawn Tennis Club where she was first coached by H. Lawrence and later by Charles Martin and [Harold Mahony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Mahony "Harold Mahony").[[a]](#cite_note-lawntennis-3) She won her first senior singles title in 1893 at [Ilkley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilkley "Ilkley").[[2]](#cite_note-odnb-2) Between 1893 and 1917 she participated in 21 Wimbledon tournaments. At her first appearance she reached the semifinals of the singles event in which she lost to [Blanche Bingley Hillyard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanche_Bingley_Hillyard "Blanche Bingley Hillyard"). She won her first singles title in 1895, defeating [Helen Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Jackson_(tennis) "Helen Jackson (tennis)") in the final of the All-Comers event.[[3]](#cite_note-4)[[b]](#cite_note-w1895-5) In that match she was down 0–5 in both sets but managed to win in straight sets.[[4]](#cite_note-chambers-6) In 1896, she successfully defended her title in the Challenge Round against [Alice Simpson Pickering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alice_Pickering "Alice Pickering"). Between 1897 and 1901 the titles were divided between Cooper Sterry (1898, 1901) and Bingley Hillyard (1897, 1899, 1900). The 1902 Challenge Round match against [Muriel Robb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muriel_Robb "Muriel Robb") was halted on the first day of play due to rainfall at 6–4, 11–13. The match was replayed in its entirety the next day and Robb won 7–5, 6–1, playing a total of 53 games which was then a record for the longest women's singles final.[[5]](#cite_note-7)[[6]](#cite_note-hedges-8) In 1908 as a mother of two she won her last singles title when she defeated [Agnes Morton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agnes_Morton "Agnes Morton") in straight sets in the All-Comers final after a seven-year hiatus and at the age of 37.[[7]](#cite_note-9)[[8]](#cite_note-collins-10) She is the oldest Wimbledon ladies’ singles champion and her record of eight consecutive singles finals stood until 1990 when [Martina Navratilova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martina_Navratilova "Martina Navratilova") reached her ninth consecutive singles final.[[8]](#cite_note-collins-10)[[9]](#cite_note-11)

In addition to her singles titles, Cooper Sterry also won seven All-England mixed doubles titles; five times with Harold Mahony (1894–1898)[[2]](#cite_note-odnb-2) and once with [Laurence Doherty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurence_Doherty "Laurence Doherty") (1900) and [Xenophon Casdagli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xenophon_Kasdaglis "Xenophon Kasdaglis") (1908).[[c]](#cite_note-mixeddoubles-12) In 1913 she reached the final of the first Wimbledon women's doubles event with [Dorothea Douglass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorothea_Douglass "Dorothea Douglass"), 18 years after winning her first Wimbledon title.

She won the singles title at the [Irish Lawn Tennis Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Open_(tennis) "Irish Open (tennis)") in 1895 and 1898,[[2]](#cite_note-odnb-2) a prestigious tournament at the time.[[10]](#cite_note-13) At the [1900 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1900_Summer_Olympics "1900 Summer Olympics"), where women participated for the first time, Cooper Sterry won the tennis singles event. On 11 July 1900 she defeated [Hélène Prévost](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hélène_Prévost "Hélène Prévost") in the final in straight sets and became the first female Olympic tennis champion as well as the first individual female Olympic champion. With [Reginald Doherty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reginald_Doherty "Reginald Doherty"), she won the [mixed doubles title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennis_at_the_1900_Summer_Olympics_–_Mixed_doubles "Tennis at the 1900 Summer Olympics – Mixed doubles") after a straight-sets victory in the final against Hélène Prévost and [Harold Mahony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Mahony "Harold Mahony").[[11]](#cite_note-14)[[d]](#cite_note-olympics-15) In 1901 she won the singles title at the German Championships, and in 1902 she won the Swiss Championship.[[12]](#cite_note-myers-16) Cooper Sterry remained active in competitive tennis and continued to play in championship events well into her 50s.

On 12 January 1901 she married Alfred Sterry, a solicitor, who became president of the [Lawn Tennis Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawn_Tennis_Association "Lawn Tennis Association"). They had two children: Rex (1903–81) who was the vice-chairman of the [All England Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_England_Lawn_Tennis_and_Croquet_Club "All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club") for a period of 15 years during the 1960s and 1970s and [Gwen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwen_Sterry "Gwen Sterry") (1905–87), a tennis player who participated at Wimbledon and played on Britain's [Wightman Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wightman_Cup "Wightman Cup") team.[[2]](#cite_note-odnb-2)[[13]](#cite_note-robertson-17)[[14]](#cite_note-18)[[15]](#cite_note-19)

Cooper Sterry, who had been deaf since the age of 26, died on 10 October 1966 at the age of 96, in [Helensburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helensburgh "Helensburgh"), Scotland.[[2]](#cite_note-odnb-2)[[16]](#cite_note-20)[[17]](#cite_note-21)

She was inducted into the [International Tennis Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Tennis_Hall_of_Fame "International Tennis Hall of Fame") in 2013.[[18]](#cite_note-22)

## Playing style

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Charlotte_Cooper_(tennis)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Playing style")]

Cooper Sterry had an offensive style of playing, attacking the net when the opportunity arose. She was one of a few female players of her time who served overhead. Her main strengths were her steadiness, temperament and tactical ability.[[2]](#cite_note-odnb-2) Her excellent volleying skills stood out at a time when this was still a rarity in ladies tennis.[[12]](#cite_note-myers-16)

Distribution of named craters in the Solar System as of 2017. [1] [2] [3] [4] [a] 

This is a list of craters on Venus, named by the International Astronomical Union's (IAU) Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature. All craters on Venus are named after famous women or female first names. [1] [5] (For features on Venus other than craters see, list of montes on Venus and List of coronae on Venus. [6])

As of 2017, there are 900 named craters on Venus, [1] fewer than the lunar and Martian craters but more than on Mercury. [2] [3] [4] [a] 

Other, non-planetary bodies with numerous named craters include Callisto (141), Ganymede (131), Rhea (128), Vesta (90), Ceres (90), Dione (73), Iapetus (58), Enceladus (53), Tethys (50) and Europa (41). For a full list, see List of craters in the Solar System.
